DESIGNER: What's driving that?
PM: QA found three high-severity bugs yesterday, and we already used most of our buffer time fixing the payment flow last sprint. Shipping now risks a broken checkout for a meaningful share of users.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. A specific, relevant causal claim supported by concrete evidence (bug severity, prior buffer usage). Not a hasty generalization or single-cause fallacy — it's a single well-supported reason for a narrow, proportionate conclusion.

transcript:

DERMATOLOGIST: Based on the asymmetry and the color variation I'm seeing, I'd like to biopsy it. In my experience treating thousands of cases like this, those two features together warrant a closer look.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE / borderline-but-legitimate appeal to authority. The dermatologist is a relevant expert speaking within their domain and grounding the claim in specific observable features, not bare credential-waving — this is the non-fallacious form of appeal to authority.

transcript: SPEAKER: My opponent wants you to believe his tax plan is moderate. But let's be clear about where this leads: first it's a small increase, then it's a bigger one, and within a decade we'll be taxed into the ground, just like every other place that's tried this.

ground_truth.span: first it's a small increase, then it's a bigger one, and within a decade we'll be taxed into the ground

notes: Asserts an inevitable chain from a modest first step to an extreme outcome without justifying each link.

ground_truth.span: Anyone with basic common sense can see I'm right, so I'm not going to waste time debating
I'm not going to waste time debating people who clearly don't get it

transcript:
DEFENSE ATTORNEY: My client failed the polygraph, yes. But polygraphs are well known to produce false positives under stress, and my client had just learned his mother was hospitalized that morning.

ground_truth.span: The test result speaks for itself. Innocent people don't fail lie detector tests.

notes: Assumes the test's reliability (innocent people don't fail it) as the basis for concluding guilt, when that reliability is precisely what's being challenged.

transcript:
DEBATER A: I think the merger will reduce competition in this market.
DEBATER B: That's possible, but the two companies barely overlap in product lines — one does enterprise software, the other does consumer hardware. Can you point to where the overlap actually creates a competition problem?
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. This is a legitimate, relevant rebuttal asking for the warrant behind a claim — not an appeal to ridicule or dismissal, since it engages directly with the substance.

transcript:
HOST: Some pediatricians recommend limiting screen time to one hour on weekdays.
GUEST: I get why people say that, but my grandparents didn't have screens at all and they turned out fine, so I don't think an hour a day is going to hurt anyone.

ground_truth.span: my grandparents didn't have screens at all and they turned out fine, so I don't think an hour a day is going to hurt anyone

notes: Could also be read as a hasty generalization from one family's anecdote; tagged primarily as appeal to tradition since the reasoning leans on 'how things used to be done' rather than just sample size. Annotators should accept either label as correct if justified.

transcript:
HR REP: We're proposing a new flexible PTO policy.
MANAGER: If we let people take unlimited time off, nobody's going to show up to work at all, and the whole department falls apart within a year.

ground_truth.span: If we let people take unlimited time off, nobody's going to show up to work at all, and the whole department falls apart within a year

notes: Could also be flagged as Nirvana Fallacy depending on framing; slippery slope is the better fit since the objection is about an escalating chain of consequences, not the policy's imperfection.

transcript: LECTURER: A student once asked me why we should trust peer review at all, since reviewers sometimes get things wrong. But just because the process isn't perfect doesn't mean we should throw it out — the alternative, no review at all, would let through far more errors, not fewer.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. This sentence actually rebuts a nirvana fallacy rather than committing one — it explicitly argues against rejecting an imperfect system in favor of a worse alternative.

transcript:
HOST: My guest today says raising the minimum wage kills jobs. He runs three restaurants, so listen up — he's lived it.
GUEST: That's right. I've cut staff every time my labor costs went up.

ground_truth.span: I've cut staff every time my labor costs went up

notes: Generalizing a broad economic claim from one business owner's personal experience across his three restaurants; the host's framing ('he's lived it') primes the anecdote as proof but the fallacy itself sits in the guest's generalization.

transcript: INFLUENCER: I know some of you are going to say 'where's your medical degree' — but you don't need a degree to know how your own body feels, okay? I feel amazing on this, that's the only data point that matters to me.

ground_truth.span: I feel amazing on this, that's the only data point that matters to me

notes: Personal subjective experience explicitly elevated to sole/sufficient evidence, dismissing the relevance of expertise pre-emptively (note: the pre-emptive dismissal itself borders on poisoning the well against future medical criticism, but the core fallacy in this span is the anecdote-as-proof move).

notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. Specific, hedged, quantified claim with no overgeneralization or causal leap.

ground_truth.span: I've used it for two weeks and mine's been totally fine, so I think those reports are overblown

HOST: Does the new study settle the debate on saturated fat?
GUEST: Not really — it's one cohort study, fairly large, but observational, so it shows an association, not causation. We'd want a few replications and ideally an RCT before treating this as settled.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. The guest explicitly avoids the correlation-causation leap and names the epistemic limitation directly — this is a model of fallacy-avoidance, not commission.

ground_truth.span: I don't really have an example, but that's a good thing because it means I'm a team player

notes: Assumes the conclusion (never disagreeing = being a good team player) as a premise without establishing it; could also be read loosely as a non-answer, but the specific phrasing asserts the value judgment as already settled.

transcript: NARRATOR (reading op-ed): Three independent audits over the last two years found the agency's reported numbers overstated actual outcomes by 15 to 20 percent. Based on that pattern, it's reasonable to treat next quarter's projected figures with some skepticism until a fourth audit is complete.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. A pattern across three independent audits supports a proportionate, hedged conclusion ('some skepticism,' not certainty) — this is legitimate inductive reasoning, not hasty generalization.

notes: TRUE NEGATIVE for Speaker B. Speaker B's response is a legitimate methodological challenge (dose, species relevance), not a dismissal — it directly engages the evidence rather than committing a fallacy. (Speaker A's claim might itself be a hasty generalization depending on framing, but is left unlabeled here since dose-response context is unstated; use as a discussion case for annotator calibration.)

ground_truth.span: If he's lying, he'd avoid eye contact. He's avoiding eye contact, so he must be lying.

notes: Affirms the consequent (avoiding eye contact) to conclude the antecedent (lying), ignoring other reasons someone might avoid eye contact.

SPEAKER B: Well, we're not cutting taxes, so the economy won't grow.

ground_truth.span: we're not cutting taxes, so the economy won't grow

notes: Denies the antecedent (tax cuts) to conclude the consequent is false (no growth), ignoring other paths to growth.

PLAYER A: All unicorns have horns.
PLAYER B: Right, so there must be some unicorns out there somewhere with horns.

ground_truth.span: so there must be some unicorns out there somewhere with horns

notes: Infers that members of a category exist just because a universal statement about that category is true; 'all unicorns have horns' can be true even if no unicorns exist.

MANAGER: So some juniors finished early, then?

ground_truth.span: So some juniors finished early, then?

notes: Draws an affirmative conclusion (some juniors did finish early) from two premises that are both negative or partly negative, which is never logically valid.

ground_truth.span: So clearly nobody at any level approved it.

notes: Both premises are negative (no managers, no executives), which can't validly support any conclusion about who approved it — some other role could have.

ground_truth.span: And doctors are caring people. So engineers must be caring too.

ground_truth.span: And all our best clients are local. So all local clients pay on time.

ground_truth.span: So we must be acting just like our competitors.

COORDINATOR: If it rains, we move the event indoors. The forecast says it's raining, so we're moving it indoors.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. Valid modus ponens (if A then B; A; therefore B) — not affirming the consequent, since the antecedent (rain) is what's actually confirmed.

transcript:

LEAD: There are no error codes in the log, so the sensor isn't broken.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. Valid modus tollens (if A then B; not B; therefore not A) — logically sound, not denying the antecedent.

transcript: BIOLOGY TEACHER: All mammals are warm-blooded. All dogs are mammals. Therefore, all dogs are warm-blooded.
notes: TRUE NEGATIVE. A textbook-valid categorical syllogism (Barbara form) — the middle term 'mammals' is properly distributed, unlike the undistributed-middle or four-term fallacy patterns.

transcript:
PM: We've put eight months into this feature.
